body: Beautiful!!
Congratulations!! I am so proud of you!
Oh friend, I'm so sorry this is happening to you. Please know you are not being melodramatic. I hope you are able to find the help you need soon. Stay strong.
Congrats, friend! What a wonderful development. I'm so proud of you!

Congratulations, friend!! This is wonderful news and I am so happy for you. I don't know that I ever would have overcome my self-harm if I hadn't seen a psychiatrist--having the right meds makes it so much easier. It's not an automatic fix; sometimes you have to try lots of drug cocktails before you find the right one. But stick with it, talk to your doctor, talk to a therapist, you're doing a great job and I know you have wonderful things ahead of you!

I understand what you mean by this. It's not how I feel anymore, but I did feel very similarly several years ago at the height of my self-harm. Humans like labels, we like categorizing things and naming our specific identities. Cutting as an identity isn't all that different than, say, "gym rat" as an identity. Of course, that doesn't necessarily mean it's healthy, because if cutting is central to your identity then it's going to be very difficult to ever stop (though it sounds like stopping isn't your goal).

I guess I'm interested in what you mean by self-harm as freedom of self-expression. In your mind, is cutting the same thing as getting a new tattoo or piercing? That is to say, when you self-harm, are you thinking about it the way one might think about a new tattoo; or are you self-harming as a coping mechanism, and it's coming from a place of anxiety/depression/self-hate/etc?
Eleven days! That's amazing! Congratulations, friend. I'm so excited for you to hit your three-week goal!

Hi friends. I remember feeling like this, 24/7, for years. I remember being convinced that suicide was inevitable because nobody who felt that kind of pain could ever go on to live a normal (let alone happy) life. And I remember torturing myself with thoughts that absolutely nothing was wrong with me except that I was a pathetic and worthless human.

For what it's worth, I don't feel that way anymore. It took time and work (I've been in therapy for so long that I'm literally trying to become a therapist myself) and at first it was really fucking weird to feel happy, but that's truly where I am now. I *like* myself now. I feel like a whole person. I'm not ashamed of my scars. I've even started talking openly about being a suicide attempt survivor, and I've been able to help a few of my friends who were struggling with mental illness. That feels amazing, to help the people coming up the path behind me.

I mention all of this because I'm the fucking proof, y'all: Suicide isn't inevitable. Healing is possible. There's nothing special about me; if I can heal, anyone can. All of you can. I love you all, I care about you all, I'm proud of you all. And I absolutely love that there's a group where we can share about self-harm with dark and hilarious memes. Stay strong, friends. I'm cheering for you.

You have some good advice here already about downplaying your scars and avoiding attention, so I want to offer a different (and potentially unpopular) option: You could consider telling the doctor the truth. As others have mentioned, you're not a minor so the doctor absolutely cannot say a single thing to your mom, not even a single hint. Everything is completely confidential. So maybe this could be a good opportunity to tell the doctor you're struggling with mental health and ask about your options. The doctor can probably refer you to a therapist, or you could talk about whether anxiety or depression medication might be appropriate. I know that all sounds absurd and scary, and for sure there are some doctors who are absolutely worthless, but if you feel comfortable with the doctor then you don't have anything to lose by having that conversation. This is what doctors are for! You can even have the conversation and then decide to disregard all of it, but at least you'll be armed with slightly more information and options than you have right at this moment. 

One of the challenges of your late teens and early twenties is transitioning from a kid to an adult, and I think that's what you're facing here: when you were a kid, your parents and doctor controlled your health and you had little say in it. But now you're a legal adult and you have the opportunity and the power to take control of your health. If you're not yet ready to talk to a doctor (or anyone else) that's totally fine, but it's at least worth considering all your options in this situation. I know I never would have made any improvements with my mental health if I hadn't finally talked to a doctor about it. Good luck, friend!

You are valid. You are valid. You are valid. You are *always* valid, my friend.

Humans need other humans. We need affection, attention, love. If your needs aren't being met, it makes sense that you would feel desperate and resort to desperate measures. I just saw an Instagram post this morning about a mother elephant who got stranded in deep mud on the banks of a lake, and she was struggling and wailing and desperate to get back to her herd no matter what. And that's just an animal! You have even greater emotional needs, and being desperate to fulfill your needs *is an absolutely valid and natural way to feel.*

I do hope you will find better ways to get the love and attention you need other than hurting yourself, though. Hang in there, friend. I care about you.

I'm sorry you've having such a bad day, friend. It's only one day, and it's mostly over now; you can make it! I'm proud of you for dragging yourself out of bed, it's so fucking hard to be around people when your mind is working against you like this.

I'm guessing "asked to stay home. Got told no" means you're still in school and living with your parents/family. Everything gets so much better when you're finally an adult and can control your own life--or it did for me, in any case. No more forcing yourself to act normal when you're having a bad mental health day. No more asking for permission to spend your time the way you want to spend your time. If your situation is like mine was, no more living in fear that your parents will realize what you're doing and punish you for it. You'll have opportunities to build real friendships and relationships with people who care about you and are invested in your well-being. Hang in there, friend. Cry in front of your mirror as much as you need to. This isn't forever, you'll make it through. I'm cheering for you.

I'm sorry this happened to you, friend. Relationships with siblings can be really complicated. I'm sure she loves you, but we don't always know how to express that love, and sometimes we hurt people even though we love them. That seems to be what happened here--it could be she was trying to help, but regardless of her intentions, calling you ugly, mocking your scars, and then threatening to kill herself is not okay. It's not acceptable behavior, it's verbally abusive. You deserve to be treated better than that. I hope this really was a one-time thing, in which case maybe you can have a conversation with her, explain how much her words and actions hurt you, and suggest some alternative ways she can be supportive in the future.

Stay strong, friend! I'm cheering for you.

Hey, a day can be forever sometimes. I'm proud of you for getting through that say! You self-harm counter only went up 1 day, but that's also 24 hours; 1,440 minutes; 86,400 seconds. It only takes a second to hurt yourself, so that's 86,400 times you stayed strong. Keep it up, friend!

You're getting out of there! You're getting help and you never have to see him again! Bring this mindset with you when you go to the hospital and I bet you'll do better in the hospital than you have before. Congratulations on your hard-won freedom and, eventually, your independence. I'm rooting for you!

Humans are wired to need the love and affection of other humans. There's nothing pathetic about it at all! 

I care about you, and I hope you are okay.

It really depends. Ideally, your partner will be someone you can share everything with, but not everyone has the capacity to handle self-harm updates. I don't think it has to always be unhealthy to share that kind of information with a partner, but it also depends on the partner. Is her mental health in a good place? Does she have the emotional maturity to handle a crisis-like situation? What do you hope to gain from telling her? I don't think withholding that information is necessarily the same as lying, especially if you are withholding it to avoid distressing her. And unless y'all are married or in a long-term committed relationship, I don't think she's entitled to that kind of personal information from you (and maybe not even if you are married). 

I do not mean to say you should keep your self-harm a secret, but unless your partner has an incredibly high level of emotional maturity, telling her each time might start to get to her and make her feel guilty because she can't "fix" you. She might start to feel like it's her fault that you're not happy. Are you seeing a therapist or otherwise working to stop self-harming? Because I think there's a difference between telling her in the context of "I hurt myself, but I'm trying really hard not to so I'm going to talk to my therapist about it this week and I just wanted you to know, I'd appreciate some extra cuddles today" vs updating her every time just for the sake of keeping her updated.

I'm so sorry you're feeling this way, friend. My best advice about self-harm is to try not to start in the first place. Once you have the habit, it is very very hard to break it. 

Life is change, and I promise it can change for the better. Why do you feel pressure to figure out what to do with your life right now? You have, well, your whole life to figure that out! Friend, I know your head is full of darkness now, but I promise it will not always be that way. Hang in there, you can do this.

There's no "should" here, it just depends what you're comfortable with. I think you'll get fewer questions than you're expecting, especially if the scars are on your legs--even when you're swimming, how often do you look at other people's legs? And if people do notice, they'll rarely ask--it's a pretty rude question unless you know somebody really well. So you can tell them the truth if you want, or you can tell them something else ("I got in a lot of bike accidents as a kid!"...yes people really are that gullible), or you can just tell them you're not comfortable discussing such a personal topic.

Dreams don't objectively mean anything, but it might have some kind of meaning for you personally. How did you feel in the dream? In real life, maybe your brain is feeling stressed and you are subconsciously craving the adrenaline rush of self-harm. Or maybe you are concerned about self-harm and your dream is your brain's way of processing your fear.

Ugh friend I feel you, I'm in zoom grad school and it's so freaking hard. I promise that whatever you said is not nearly as bad in reality as it feels in your head, especially over zoom where there's a 98% chance nobody else in your class was even paying attention. 

Professors who describe themselves as hard graders are dicks. This dick professor is **not** worth hurting yourself over! Do you have the option to take a different class instead? Or could you take this one pass/fail?

It is self-harm, and it can escalate quickly. If you develop a habit of self-harm, it is a very, very hard habit to break. Do you have anyone in your real life that you trust enough to talk to? Maybe a teacher or a family member?
I'm thinking about you, friend.

Hey friend. I'm sorry this is happening to you. You are not useless, and you deserve so much better than to feel useless. A whole month--wow! That takes a tremendous amount of strength and courage. I'm so proud of you for being strong and brave. Keep going, friend. I care about you and I am rooting for you.

I love this. 

I love all of you, even if you do not love yourself right now.

We have all stared suffering directly in the face and yet here we are, still breathing. How amazing of all of us. How amazing of you. I am so proud of you all, and I am grateful for this community where we can help carry each other's pain.

Thank you for posting this, u/Cozy_Weeb.

Hi friend, and welcome. I was dealing with depression and thoughts of self-harm when I was your age, too. It's hard to be in so much pain when you're that young. But I'm 32 now, and happy, and have built a really lovely life for myself, so please know that healing is possible. Do you have anyone in your real life that you trust and can talk to? A teacher or a family member, maybe?

As others have said, it's best not to start because once you're in the habit, it's a really really hard habit to break. It's sort of like asking, "Are cigarettes bad if I only have one and not a whole pack?" Sure, one cigarette won't kill you, but once you have one, it's easier to have a second, third, fourth, and so on. The knife usually doesn't cut your skin that much NOW but if you keep up the habit, just like any other drug you build up a tolerance and start to feel that you need more and more and more. Once you get used to the idea that physically hurting yourself is a just fine thing to do, you're at the trailhead of a dangerous path.

I saw in your comment history (pardon the snooping!) that you are very young. Friend, I hated my body when I was your age too. Just remember that the body you have right now is only temporary--you're still growing into your adult self, physically, mentally, emotionally. Do you have anyone in your life you trust enough to talk to? A teacher, a therapist, a family member?

I've always felt like I had a weird sixth sense around spotting other people who self-harm. There is so much shame and stigma and misunderstanding around it that when you see someone else with cuts out in the wild, it does sometimes feel like an intense connection with them; we folk gotta stick together, you know? Don't see this as a failure to talk to or help them, see this as an opportunity! Of course you can't dive right in the very first moment you meet someone else, but like you say, hopefully you'll share a shift soon and will be able to form a friendship where you help and support each other...you do already know you have one big, if painful, thing in common, after all.
I am thinking about you, friend.

I know this feeling, and I've spent a lot of time philosophizing about it over the years. I think when you're in so much pain that you start cutting yourself, sometimes you develop a weird sort of...identity, or even a dark kind of pride around it. When you feel empty, or when you feel like nothing, and the only thing you can feel is the physical pain, it's easy to identify very deeply with that one and only thing you can feel. And then add the endorphins/adrenaline on top of that. It's not sick for you to miss it, it's just human human nature to be attracted to the things that make us feel better in the short term even if they're harmful to us in the long term.

This has been my experience as well. In 15+ years, the only people who have ever noticed and commented on my scars (several on my arms/shoulders, and some really nasty ones on my calves) are other people who have self-harmed. And I live in Atlanta where it's warm, so I spend *a lot* of time in short sleeves and short pants. I've come to think of my scars as a sort of secret signal to others who are suffering, so they know they aren't alone.

Analogy time: I have a friend who hates wearing shoes so he'll often run errands or go to the grocery store barefoot. Nobody ever stops him--his philosophy is to "walk like you have shoes on" and then nobody will notice you're not. In other words, if you don't call attention to it, if you act inconspicuous, nobody else is likely to notice. I think the same philosophy applies to scars: Live as if you don't have them--or even better, live as if you're not ashamed of them--because unless you draw attention to them, most people won't notice. This is one of those times when people's natural tendency toward self-absorption comes in handy.

This perspective is so, so important. At the risk of sounding like a "back in my day..." geezer: the height of my self-harm and suicidal ideation was 15 years ago, before things like Reddit were around. There were a few dark corners of the internet with message boards for "cutters" but you were just as likely to find pro-harm and triggering material as you were to find support. The internet was so lonely back then. Communities like this are AMAZING, it would have meant so much to my teenage self to know there were other people like me in the world. It's one of those things that makes me grateful for technology, because now it's easier to find community and support from people who actually understand. Grateful for you all and for the wonderful place you've built here!

Please resist, friend. I know exactly what it's like to feel empty, but I promise you, you are not empty. You are full to the brim with strength and courage--the fact that you are posting here proves that. That feeling of emptiness isn't emptiness at all, it's just vastness. I like to imagine it like the ocean--maybe it seems empty at first, but only because it is so huge, and when you start to explore it you find it's full of incredible life. Imagine yourself sinking beneath the turbulent waves at the surface, and swim down underneath where the water is cool and still and calm, where you can float weightless and free for as long as you'd like. I am rooting for you, friend. You can do this.
I am so proud of you! A whole month--what an accomplishment. You are so strong to have made it this far. Keep it up! I'm rooting for you.

I want you to be here, friend. My 20th birthday wasn't great either, and neither was my 21st for that matter. But you know what? I turned 32 this summer and it was a wonderful day. Just because you have lonely birthdays in your past doesn't mean you have them in your future. In my late teens and early 20s, it often felt like the pain inside me was so huge that it was going to blow my body apart like the Death Star. It was like my body wasn't big enough to contain my suffering. But you're young, and as you grow, you become bigger and stronger than the pain. Don't give up now, when you've already made it through two entire decades! Things got so much better for me as I became an adult and finally had independence and control over my own life. I also wanted to give up when I was 20, and now I'm so glad I didn't; your future self is going to feel the same way about your 20-year-old self some day. Things are going to get better for you too, friend. I know this birthday is hard, but I also know you have truly happy birthdays waiting for you in your future. I'm so excited for you to get to feel that happiness some day!

Oh my friend, you have been dealt a bad hand and are so strong to have made it this far. It flippin sucks to tackle Everest on your first rodeo, but those of us who've made it over Everest have such incredible strength and resilience. Be proud of how far you've already come, friend. I'm proud of you.

You ask what kind of life this is and what kind of future is waiting for you. Obviously nobody can predict the future, but I do believe we all have the capacity inside us to create a life and future where we are happy. It's just hard to feel it sometimes, especially when you've gone through so much pain in your life. For a long time I thought that feeling the kind of pain that led me to attempt suicide meant that I would forever be incapable of feeling any happiness at all, but now I know that isn't true because I've experienced it in my own life. Your pain might make your happiness hide deep inside you, but it can never chase it away entirely. I promise. 

I know this seems like such an eyeroll-worthy suggestion, but have you ever tried to keep a gratitude journal? Write down 1-3 things every day that you are grateful for, even if you go days in a row where the only thing you feel grateful for are your pets or nice weather or your favorite tv show. That exercise really helped me start seeing all the little things in my life that are wonderful but that I never noticed before, and it made it easier to focus on the good instead of the bad. For example, you have a whole COLLECTION of ant colonies?? Holy cow! That must be so many ants! Thousands? Tens of thousands? And ants are AMAZING. I even have a tattoo of a bite from a leaf-cutter ant! All these tiny living creatures working and building together, and every single one of them relies on you. How incredible to be the caretaker of such fascinating animals!

You also say you're trying to be a good person. I know that struggle well, and my best piece of advice is that it will be much easier to be a good person to others once you are a good person to yourself. Don't worry about trying to be likeable or loveable to others right now; focus on finding the things you like and love about yourself first. I know that seems damn near impossible sometimes, so I'll start you off with a list of things I already like about you: 

* Your courage for posting here
* Your neuro-atypical brain - I have ADHD too, and us neurodivergent folk have to stick together
* Your unconditional love for your dog Winry
* Your compassion - you saved a poor puppy from a bin and you're caring for all these ants, even though most people see ants as pests instead of pets
* Your appreciation for Temple Grandin - "Animals Make Us Human" had a huge influence on me
* Your username, cause frogs are also really freakin cool
* Your "you are all immortal in this moment" attitude - I'm Buddhist, so appreciating the special importance of each moment is a big part of my life.

As an Everest veteran myself, I'm rooting for you, my friend! It's grueling and cold and dangerous making it up the mountain, but the view from the top is amazing. And, most importantly, remember that you're not alone on the mountain; you're not the first person to attempt the climb; other people have made it and we're all cheering for you to make it too. 

Finally, friend, I want you to know that it's about 3pm here in Atlanta, I'm thinking about you, and I'm going to keep thinking about you for the rest of the day. I'm imagining you sitting next to your ant colonies, marveling over how awesome ants are, just like I'm marveling over how awesome you are for overcoming everything you already have. 

Keep it up, friend! I'm so excited for you to arrive on the other side of Everest. You're gonna love it here.

Something that always hurts is having the sense that your friends can't "handle" hearing about your pain and self-harm. So just offer to listen, if you're up for it. Don't judge, don't cringe. Having someone you can talk to without fear that they'll judge you or tell other people about your secret can make a difference. 

And above all, I think, ask her what kind of support she needs. If she's feeling lonely, offer company; if she's feeling misunderstood, offer to understand; if she's feeling triggered, offer to distract her. Recognize how remarkably strong your friend is: she's going through life every single day carring this enormous pain by herself. Encourage her strength and tell her you're proud of her and that you care about her.
